agv.text: Psychology has 'fatigue insensitivity': the more tired you are, the less you notice, because cortisol masks the signal. By the time you 'feel tired', you've already been overloaded for a long time. That's why scheduled breaks beat 'rest by feeling' — that's why this app exists.

agw.title: Productivity isn't a daily new record
agw.text: Output curves naturally have peaks and valleys. You're not a machine set to constant output — you're a person with rhythms. Today producing 20% less than yesterday isn't necessarily failure — it might just be recovery. Allow the dips, and the long-term curve actually rises.

agx.title: Emotional labor is labor too
agx.text: Tech work isn't just code. It's communicating with PMs, negotiating with bosses, coordinating with teams, replying to endless messages — all emotional labor, draining attention and psychic energy. 'Not wanting to do anything' after work isn't fragility; the brain genuinely has no battery. Treat it as real depletion.

agy.title: The opposite of work isn't rest — it's passivity
agy.text: Real rest is active: you decide to stop, you decide what moves, you decide what to look at. Passively scrolling shorts, scrolling feeds — that's not rest. The brain is still being driven by the stream. These 5 minutes, please do something actively: stand, look far, do a few moves.

agz.title: Screen brightness isn't a health metric
agz.text: Even a perfectly tuned screen can't replace the eye's need for real depth. Eyes evolved to alternate near and far focus; long-term single distance stiffens ciliary muscles. This break: leave the screen, look at something 'real' — outside the window, far away, three-dimensional, natural.

aha.title: Your neck isn't a cantilever beam
aha.text: In engineering, the longer the cantilever, the easier it breaks. When you bend your head, your neck is a cantilever holding a 5-kilogram skull — and it's been holding it for 8 hours. Solution: raise the screen so eye level meets the screen midpoint; tuck chin lightly; ears over shoulders. A simple geometric correction saves you a decade of neck rehab.

ahb.title: How many times did you laugh today?
ahb.text: Adults laugh on average 17 times a day — less than half what 6-year-olds do. Laughter activates the parasympathetic system, releases endorphins, lowers cortisol — free mental maintenance. This break, watch something that makes you laugh. Even silly photos of yourself.

ahc.title: You're not sitting for your salary
ahc.text: You think the extra 2 hours bring extra wages. But discount future neck pain, lumbar strain, vision loss back to today — those 2 hours are a net loss. You're not earning; you're borrowing health to plug a future hole. Worth it? Think honestly.

ahd.title: Your body remembers every act of consistency
ahd.text: Stand 1 minute today, stretch 30 seconds tomorrow, drink an extra cup the day after — each looks negligible. But the body is a long-term memory system. In 30 days it returns the favor: steadier energy, less ache, better sleep. Compounding, not pointless.

ahe.title: Why does rest leave you more tired?
ahe.text: If your 'rest' is doomscrolling for 2 hours, that's not rest — it's low-quality fatigue stacking. Restorative rest needs at least one of: physical relaxation, mental clearing, emotional flow. Eight hours of anxious dreams, you wake up tired. This break: pick one of those three and do it for real.

ahf.title: You're not introverted — you're depleted
ahf.text: Many people just want to be alone after work and wonder if they're 'antisocial' or 'cold'. More likely: your daytime attention and emotion got drained. Allow yourself quiet. Not every day needs socializing. When energy returns, 'wanting to see people' returns naturally — not a flaw, a rhythm.

ahg.title: Write the anxiety down
ahg.text: Anxiety in the head loops endlessly. Writing it down adds a break statement. Studies show that 3 minutes of writing down current worries significantly reduces cognitive interference at work. If your mind is loud today, this break, get a sheet of paper. Dump them out. Lighten the load.

ahh.title: Standing up = restart
ahh.text: When the computer hangs, restart often fixes it. Same for humans. Stuck on the same problem for 3 hours? Five minutes of standing is usually more effective than another 30 of staring. Not superstition — cognitive science. Body state changes force the brain to switch modes.

ahi.title: Be a real person for a minute
ahi.text: In offices, it's easy to become 'roles': employee, subordinate, lead. But you're not a role — you're a real person with a body, family, dreams. This break, briefly step out of the role: feel your pockets, think of someone you love, look at the sky. Then go back and play the role again.

ahj.title: You don't always need to be producing
ahj.text: The industrial-era wage system trained us to think 'time = output = value'. Creative work doesn't run that way. The best ideas appear during walks, showers, cooking — not while staring at the screen. Pausing now might be precisely the preparation for the next breakthrough.

ahk.title: Your lower back is a load-bearing wall
ahk.text: The lumbar spine carries most of your upper body's weight — the body's load-bearing wall. If it fails, the house comes down. Lowest-cost reinforcements: stand straight, avoid crossed legs, get up regularly. They look trivial — five years from now you'll be grateful.

ahl.title: Your colleagues probably need this break too
ahl.text: Look around. They're stuck in the same posture you are. When you stand up this time, you can ask: 'Anyone want to grab water with me?' That's not socializing-as-waste — it's collective maintenance. Studies show group breaks lower stress and improve team collaboration.

ahm.title: You're not 'in demand', you're being consumed
ahm.text: If a job has you on call 24/7, that's not 'being valued' — it's missing boundaries. Reserving distraction-free time is a basic professional survival skill. This 5 minutes, mute your notifications. Let the world wait. It won't collapse.

ahn.title: Tech debt and body debt
ahn.text: Tech debt accumulates and eventually drags down the whole project. Body debt does the same. Skipping a stretch, one more late night, skipping a glass of water — each invisible alone, but five years of accumulated interest is brutal. Only one repayment plan: start now, pay regularly.

aho.title: What is 'just-right' work?
aho.text: Psychology calls it 'flow' — neither bored nor anxious, perfectly challenged. Highest happiness, highest output. But flow needs recovery: a real break roughly every 90 minutes lets the next round happen. This recovery is preparation for the next flow.

ahp.title: Push the screen 30 cm further away
ahp.text: The healthy eye-to-screen distance is 60–70 cm. Most people lean in unconsciously, dropping it to 30–40 cm — and eyes, neck, and shoulders all suffer. Coming back from this break, push the chair back, push the screen back. Not overcorrection. Just return.

ahq.title: You don't have to reply instantly
ahq.text: Messaging tools fooled us into 'instant reply = professional'. The actual pros leave themselves a buffer: don't reply in seconds, don't drop the ball either. This break, allow yourself not to check messages. The world won't stall because you're 5 minutes late — but you will if you're always online.

ahr.title: Good moods are maintained
ahr.text: Good moods rarely appear from nowhere. They're maintained by small acts: getting sunlight, hydration, real food, movement, seeing someone you care about. Bad moods often come from skipping these. This break, pick one and patch it in.

ahs.title: Don't wait until 'after this is done'
ahs.text: 'After this is done I'll exercise.' 'After this is done I'll sleep more.' 'After this is done I'll get a checkup.' That 'done' never comes. The only window you can crack is in the now. This 5 minutes is that window.

aht.title: Work isn't your identity
aht.text: Taking 'I'm an engineer at company X' too seriously makes you forget 'I'm a person who hurts and tires'. Lose the company, you're still you. Lose the body, you're not. This break, briefly step out of the professional identity.

ahu.title: Did you thank your body today?
ahu.text: Your heart has been beating since the day you were born. Lungs breathing, stomach digesting, kidneys filtering, eyes seeing, legs walking — no KPI, no bonus, never on strike. This break: hand on your chest, say thanks. Sounds corny — actually it works.

ahv.title: Stress isn't the problem. Chronic stress is.
ahv.text: Short-term stress sharpens you, raises output. The problem is when 'short' becomes 'chronic' — immunity drops, inflammation climbs, memory thins. The remedy is to insert 'recovery periods'. This break is one. Use it well.

ahw.title: After deep work, deep rest
ahw.text: You just finished a real focus session — give yourself a real recovery to match. Bad rest makes the next round harder; good rest makes it deeper. A simple symmetry: what you give the body, the body returns.

ahx.title: Dim the screen, brighten the world
ahx.text: Bright screens at night suppress melatonin and delay sleep. Tonight: lower brightness one notch, switch to warm tones (Night Shift). Sleep quality improves visibly — your brain's 'cleaners' get to do their job properly.

ahy.title: Anxiety hates motion
ahy.text: Anxiety's least favorite thing is movement. When you stand, breathe, walk, look far — anxiety scatters, because it needs you stuck to grow. A simple anti-hack: use the body's motion to break the mind's freeze.

ahz.title: You're already doing something remarkable
ahz.text: Just by reading this reminder during a busy workload — and considering whether to actually stand up — you've already beaten most people. Most just keep sitting on autopilot. Pausing on purpose is the elite version of self-discipline. This stand is a reward, not a chore.

aia.title: The 30 minutes before logoff
aia.text: In the last half-hour of work, please don't start new tasks. Use it for three things: close out today, set up tomorrow, buffer for the body. Specifically: list tomorrow's 3 most important things, close all non-essential tabs, breathe deeply for 3 minutes. A quiet habit of high performers.

aib.title: The truth about time management
aib.text: Time management isn't packing the calendar full — it's knowing what NOT to do. Reserving 'do nothing' gaps is an advanced skill. These 5 minutes are today's most valuable time-management experiment.

aic.title: Split today into three
aic.text: High performers tend to split a day into 3 phases: morning focus (hardest things), afternoon execution (energy-spending things), late-day wrap-up (communication and sorting). One real rest between each. Closer to how the brain actually runs than 'grind 10 hours straight'. Try it.

aid.title: The two faces of muscle memory
aid.text: Muscle memory is an engineer's favorite phrase — good muscle memory makes you type fast. But bad muscle memory forms too: hunched shoulders, tilted head, one shoulder up. One minute of reverse correction daily slowly overwrites the bad memory. Body remembers correct form.

aie.title: Lonely work needs deliberate connection
aie.text: If you went 8 hours today without really 'speaking with someone' — only typing, screens, messages — the brain feels covert loneliness. Even sending a text to family, offering a colleague a snack, are meaningful connection. We're social animals, not terminals.

aif.title: Standing up = oxygen for the brain
aif.text: Standing pumps blood harder; brain oxygen rises 10–15%. That's why some people prefer 'standing meetings' — heads really are clearer. If you got stuck, standing might be the fastest unsticker.

aig.title: You don't need to improve every day
aig.text: The advice says 'improve 1% daily'. In real life, some days you can only hold the line — or even fall back a little. That's normal, not failure. Treat 'maintenance' as progress: keeping body, mood, relationships steady already beats most people.

aih.title: Boundaries between work and life
aih.text: Still thinking about work after you log off? That's a missing boundary. Easiest way to build one: a fixed 'switch ritual' — close laptop, wash hands, change clothes, walk 5 minutes. The brain knows 'work is over'. This midday break is the same drill.

aii.title: Your accomplishment list
aii.text: Spend 30 seconds reviewing what you finished today — even if it's a few emails, a small bug, one PR. The brain naturally focuses on what's left undone and ignores what's done. Counting completed items deliberately makes returning to work feel calmer.

aij.title: The science of deep breathing
aij.text: Slow breathing (under 6 per minute) activates the vagus nerve — heart rate down, blood pressure stable, cortisol down. Not meditation magic, well-replicated physiology. Try now: 4 in, 6 out, 6 cycles. Within a minute you'll feel it.

aik.title: You don't have to be the hero
aik.text: You don't have to 'carry' the team, 'fight' for the company, 'hold up' the family. Set the hero pressure down for a moment. Be an ordinary person who needs water and a stretch. Ordinary is fine. Ordinary is sustainable.

ail.title: Hallways are more useful than you think
ail.text: The office hallway isn't just a corridor — it's a natural 'movement space'. Two laps = 100–200 steps, much better than zoning out at the desk. Stairs are even better. One floor up and down beats coffee.

aim.title: Microexpressions decide today's energy
aim.text: Furrowed brow, clenched teeth, pursed lips — these microexpressions feed back into mood. Force your mouth corners up for 30 seconds and the nervous system actually reads 'mood improving'. Sounds absurd. Replicated by multiple studies. Try it this break.

ain.title: The real cost of getting sick
ain.text: One bad cold: 3–7 days of zero output, hundreds to thousands in medical fees, months of weakened immunity. A serious neck flare: physical therapy, anxiety, weeks of disrupted work. Those are 'if not' costs of prevention. Every voluntary break flattens those invisible bills.

aio.title: You're not 'squeezing it out'
aio.text: Treating work as something you 'squeeze out' makes you drier and drier. Try a different metaphor: work as something that 'flows' — you just clear the channel and let it pass. Active rest then isn't a burden — it's clearing the channel.

aip.title: Survival philosophy in office buildings
aip.text: Surviving office life in big cities isn't easy: 1–2 hour commutes, takeout, 8 hours sitting, late-night work. What you can do isn't change all that — it's carve small spaces in every gap: a glass of water, a stretch, a deep breath. Stacked, those gaps become your survival strategy.

aiq.title: Before changing a line of code, change posture once
aiq.text: Next time you tackle a tricky piece of code, do one thing first: stand, stretch, deep breath. Let the body enter 'ready state'. Studies show that work starting from 'action readiness' enters flow over 30% faster than cold starts.

air.title: Saying no is part of health
air.text: Learning to say 'no' — to overtime, to last-minute requests, to time-eating meetings — is a core health skill. When the body isn't being demanded of infinitely, it can supply the energy you actually need. This break is a gentle 'no' to work.

ais.title: Feet are the body's most-forgotten part
ais.text: All-day shoes, all-day pedals — feet are forgotten longest. Take shoes off. Curl toes, spread toes — 10 each. The feet are dense with neural reflex zones; activating them improves whole-body circulation. A quiet luxury.

ait.title: Your job won't protect you
ait.text: However nice the company's checkup package, year-end bonus, or benefits — none of them carry your body's pain or illness for you. The only protection is the small things you do daily for yourself. This break isn't from the company — it's from you to you.

aiu.title: You don't have to prove you're busy
aiu.text: Modern workplaces have a strange culture: busy = important = valuable. So many subconsciously perform 'busy'. The actually-productive people understand the wisdom of 'looking unbusy': they focus, then truly rest, no theatre. This break, drop the 'must look busy' act.

aiv.title: Exercise is a free antidepressant
aiv.text: Thirty minutes of moderate exercise is roughly equivalent to first-line antidepressants for mild-to-moderate depression. Mechanism: BDNF promotion, serotonin and dopamine modulation. You don't need a gym — brisk walk, stairs, stretches. Today's movement is mood insurance.

aiw.title: You've already done well enough
aiw.text: Whatever today's progress, you've already done well enough. Not consolation — fact. You got up, went out, typed, solved, survived the commute. That beats every 'didn't even try' alternative. One minute of self-acknowledgment, then continue.

aix.title: Your rest serves the team too
aix.text: If you think 'resting will hold the team back', you're wrong. Studies repeatedly show: regular breaks → steadier output, fewer errors, better collaboration. Code written by an exhausted person often costs others 3× the time to fix. You rest 5 minutes, the team nets 15.

aiy.title: Neck and emotion are wired together
aiy.text: Neck tension and anxiety often co-fire — they share neural pathways. So relaxing the neck releases anxiety too. Try now: drop shoulders fully, tuck chin lightly, breathe deep × 3. Mood improves faster than you'd expect.

aiz.title: Do something useless
aiz.text: Give yourself 1 minute today for something completely useless: watch a cloud, smell your coffee, say something to the dust on the windowsill. 'Useless' is the heart of recovery. A person who only does 'useful' will be drained by 'useful'.

aja.title: The 30-second restart protocol
aja.text: Next time you're stuck for 5+ minutes, try the simplest protocol: stand, breathe deep × 3, look far for 20 seconds, sit. 30 seconds. Yes, that's it. Forces the brain to switch networks and re-sort clues. Far more effective than another 30 minutes of staring.

ajb.title: How many times did you save yourself today?
ajb.text: No one will really remember how many lines of code you wrote today — but your body remembers how many times you saved it. Every stand-up, every glass of water, every deep breath is insurance for future-you. This is one more.

ajc.title: The adult's gift
ajc.text: The biggest gift of being an adult is you finally get to decide how to treat yourself. No more parents, teachers, bosses telling you to 'just hold on a bit longer'. You're grown — you can decide 'now is the time to rest'. This break is a small kindness from you to grown-up-you.

ajd.title: Everything great needs recovery
ajd.text: Top athletes spend 30–50% of training plans on recovery, not training. Top chess players play less than 4–5 hours of competition daily. Top scientists force themselves to walk, nap, journal. Everyone who treats 'recovery' as part of the work eventually wins. So can you.

aje.title: You don't need to feel guilty
aje.text: If 'I should be doing something more' creeps in during rest — that's workism guilt, not fact. You don't feel guilty about drinking water or blinking, so you shouldn't feel guilty about 5 minutes of rest. It's a baseline body right.

ajf.title: The reality outside the screen
ajf.text: The world inside the screen tricks us into thinking it's the whole world — but it's just one window curated by an algorithm. This break, leave the window for 5 minutes. Look at the real, three-dimensional, un-pushed reality. The tree outside, the cat downstairs, the hallway light — that's what your eyes actually want to see.

ajg.title: Give today back to yourself
ajg.text: Work occupied most of today, but a piece is yours. These 5 minutes, those 10, an hour tonight — those are the part you can hold. Take those 'small times' seriously. Stacked up, they're the proof you weren't fully swallowed by work.

ajh.title: You're not a 24/7 service
ajh.text: Servers need to be 24/7. You need 8 quality hours of work + 16 of recovery. If your job is pushing you toward 24/7, the problem isn't you — it's the configuration. People who can carve rest out of the system are the ones who last.

aji.title: Re-understand 'enough'
aji.text: What you did today is already 'enough' — no more, no perfection, no surpassing required. 'Enough' isn't lowering the bar; it's accepting that humans have limits. This break is a sign of respect for 'enough'.

ajj.title: One last reminder
ajj.text: You've seen hundreds of these reminders. They all say roughly the same thing: stand, drink, stretch, look far, breathe deep. Repetition isn't pointless — your body needs these every day. This time again: stand, drink, stretch, look far, breathe deep. Then go back, seriously and proudly, to the work you're doing. You deserve all of this.
